1072.title: The divine dance
1072.hook: Greek fathers described the three persons as dwelling in one another, like a round dance
1072.howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant theologians use the word perichoresis when they teach about the Trinity, and some churches have icons and hymns that speak of the three persons dwelling in one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the filioque: and the Son, said in the creed in the West, not the East. Your line was one word, long argument.

A circle of people at a wedding, arms on each other's shoulders, stepping left, then right. Nobody in the circle is the center. Nobody leads for long. If one person stops, the whole ring feels it. And if you ask where the dance is, you can't point to any one dancer. It's in all of them, and between them. Some Christian writers have reached for exactly that picture to talk about God. Not a ruler on a throne, not a triangle on a whiteboard: a ring of movement. Like every picture of the Trinity, it falls short, but in a lively way.

Perichoresis. Greek Christian writers used it for something Jesus says in John's Gospel. He asks Philip: "Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?" Not beside. In. Later, praying for his friends, he widens it: "as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." Teachers in the Greek-speaking churches, John of Damascus among them, used perichoresis to name that mutual in-ness: Father, Son and Spirit each dwelling in the others, without blurring into one another and without being split apart. Each makes room for the others, and is at home in them. Now the dance. In English the word sounds like choreography, and some modern writers have run with that: God as a round dance, three persons moving in one movement. Others point out that the root is about going around and making room, not dancing, and would rather keep the picture loose. Both agree on what it's for. God is not a lonely thing. Before there was anything, Christians say, there was already giving and receiving, love going out and coming back. And then the prayer: that they also may be one in us. The circle has a gap, and the gap is held open. Christians differ on how far to push that. Orthodox teachers speak boldly of people being drawn into God's life; others put it more carefully. Either way, the ring in this picture is not closed.
screen: `I IN THE FATHER, THE FATHER IN ME.`
`A RING WITH A GAP HELD OPEN.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and turn slowly all the way around, a full breath for each step; if not, trace a slow circle with one hand. As you turn, think of the people who make room for you, and the people you make room for. If you pray, say the line from John, that they also may be one in us; if not, let the circle be the whole of it.
Perichoresis. The persons of the Trinity dwelling in one another, each making room for the others: some say, like a dance.
Your line: god is a dance. A ring, with a gap held open. Go gently.

1073.title: Out of nothing
1073.hook: creation out of nothing: the world isn't God and isn't an accident, but a gift
1073.howItsDone: Christians confess God as maker in the creeds, which begin with God the Father, maker of heaven and earth, and some give thanks before meals or at the start of the day for what they receive.

segments.voice: Yesterday, perichoresis: Father, Son and Spirit dwelling in one another, a ring held open. Your line was god is a dance.

A potter needs clay. A carpenter needs wood. A cook needs at least an egg. The makers we meet start with something already there, and shape it. So Christians have asked a strange question: when God made the world, what was the clay? The first line of the Bible doesn't stop to say: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." No workshop, no pile of material, no rival standing by. Christian teaching came to answer with three words. Today: out of nothing.

Out of nothing. In Latin, ex nihilo. The teaching is that God didn't shape the world from something already lying around. Before creation there was God, and nothing else. The letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear." Paul, in Romans, describes God as one who "calleth those things which be not as though they were." A voice, and then a world. Christian teachers draw two lines from this. First: the world is not God. It isn't a piece of God broken off, or God's body. A tree is a tree, a river is a river; they're made, and God is the maker. Second: the world is not an accident. Nothing forced God's hand. There was no raw stuff that had to be used up, no rival who had to be beaten. So why make anything at all? In Revelation the elders before the throne sing: "thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created." Some Christian writers read that pleasure as love: a world made because love likes to share. Between those two lines sits a third word: gift. If the world isn't God, it can be studied, used, cared for. If it isn't an accident, it was meant. Something meant, and handed over, is a gift. That turns an ordinary object into a quiet question: not just what is this for, but who gave this?

Hold whatever is closest, a mug, a pen, an apple, your own hand, and look at it as if you'd never seen it. Trace it backward, who made it, what it's made of, where that came from, until the chain runs out of answers, and stay there a moment. If you pray, give thanks for it by name; if not, just say quietly: this was given.
Out of nothing. The teaching that God made the world from no material at all: not God, not an accident, but a gift.
Your line: from nothing, for love. Every made thing can be a quiet question. See you tomorrow.

1074.title: Creation and evolution
1074.hook: many Christians accept evolution as God's way of creating; others read Genesis more literally
1074.howItsDone: Christians differ on Genesis and evolution: some churches and schools teach a young earth and six ordinary days, while others accept evolution and teach Genesis as God's account of who made the world and why.

segments.voice: Yesterday, out of nothing: the world as a gift. Your line was from nothing, for love.

A shell pressed into stone, on a museum shelf with a card beside it. A family stops to look. One child reads the card aloud. Another asks, but didn't God make the world in six days? The parents glance at each other, because they read Genesis differently, and they both go to the same church. It isn't a fight between church and science, at least not in that family. It's a question about how to read a very old page. Today: creation and evolution.

Genesis opens with days: light on the first, sky on the second, land and plants on the third, and on to the seventh, when God rests. Christians who disagree here can both call that chapter true. They differ on what kind of true. Some read the days as ordinary days and the earth as young, and see evolution as a story that doesn't fit the page; taking the text at its plainest, they say, is how they honor it. Others accept evolution as the way God made living things, over a very long time, and read the days as a pattern, a week of work and rest, telling who made the world and why, not a timetable of how. Readers of plain days point to the commandment in Exodus: "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is." Readers of a pattern point to a psalm, "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past," and to the second letter of Peter: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." And an old voice: Augustine, bishop of Hippo, wrote a book on the literal meaning of Genesis, warning Christians not to talk nonsense about the natural world in front of people who know it well, because it makes scripture look foolish. He wrote for his own day, not ours, but took the page and the world seriously. Under the arguing, both share yesterday's teaching: in six days or across ages, the world is a gift, made on purpose, by the God of every one of those days.

Your line: god of all time. Six days or long ages, one maker. That's today, done.

1075.title: Image and likeness
1075.hook: Orthodox teachers say we have God's image and grow into his likeness
1075.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians speak of growing from the image into the likeness of God, a lifelong path they call theosis, walked through prayer, the sacraments and love of neighbor; other churches speak of the same growth as sanctification.

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation and evolution: one page, read as plain days or as a pattern. Your line was god of all time.

"And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." That's Genesis, on the sixth day. Read it fast and it sounds like one idea said twice. Some readers take it that way. But some early Christian teachers slowed right down on that pair. Two words, they said, two gifts: one you're born with, one you grow into. That reading lives on in the Orthodox churches of the East, and it changes how a whole life looks. Today: image and likeness.
screen: `LET US MAKE MAN IN OUR IMAGE.`

segments.voice: Day three hundred thirty-four met the image of God in Genesis. In this reading, the image is given, whole, to every human being. The very next verse says it plainly: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." Nobody earns it. Nobody loses it. A baby has it. A prisoner has it. The person who annoys you most has it. Orthodox teachers speak of it as something like the stamp of the maker, and point to the mind and freedom that make a person a person. The likeness is not a stamp but a resemblance. It's the image starting to show in how someone actually lives: patience, mercy and love growing in them slowly, like a child growing to look like a parent. In Orthodox teaching, that growing is the whole Christian life, and it goes all the way: they call it theosis, becoming by grace like God. Paul has a line that sounds like this kind of growth: "we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory." Not in one leap. Other Christians read image and likeness as one idea said twice, and speak of growth with other words: sanctification, becoming holy. The shape is close. But the two-word reading leaves a memorable picture: a gift that's already yours, and a face you grow into.

Hold in mind one person you find hard to be around, and remember that in this teaching they carry the image too, whole. Then choose one quality you'd like to see grow in you, patience, gentleness, honesty or courage, and picture one small moment later today when it could show. If you pray, ask for help to grow toward it; if not, just hold that moment clearly.
Image and likeness. In Orthodox teaching, the image of God is given to every person; the likeness is grown into, slowly, by grace.
Your line: image given, likeness grown. It's slow work, done by grace. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1076.title: The first sin
1076.hook: Augustine taught that Adam's guilt is inherited; the Orthodox speak of inheriting mortality and a wounded nature, not guilt
1076.howItsDone: Christians speak of original sin when they teach about baptism and grace; Western churches build on Augustine's teaching of inherited guilt in different ways, while Orthodox churches teach that people inherit mortality and a wounded nature, not Adam's guilt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, image and likeness: the image given to every person, the likeness grown into. Your line was image given, likeness grown.

Why is it so easy to do the very thing you just decided not to do? The second cookie. The sharp reply. The phone, picked up again. In Romans, Paul writes: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Christian readers have heard more than a bad day in it: a pull in the grain of being human, there before anyone chooses it. Christians name where that pull comes from, and tell its story in more than one way. Today's word: original sin.
screen: `THE THING YOU DECIDED NOT TO DO.`
`THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.`

segments.voice: Original sin doesn't mean an unusual sin. It means the sin at the origin: Adam and Eve in the garden, reaching for the fruit, and everything that followed. Day three hundred thirteen called sin a condition everyone shares. Paul ties the story to all of us: "as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." Christian teaching, East and West, says something went wrong at the start and reached everyone. They differ on what was passed down. Augustine, the bishop in North Africa, taught that Adam's guilt itself is inherited: in Adam all humanity sinned, and every child is born sharing that guilt as well as its damage. In the West, Catholics and Protestants build on his reading, with different stresses. The Orthodox churches of the East tell it differently. What we inherit from Adam, they say, is not his guilt but mortality, and a wounded nature that leans toward sin. A newborn isn't guilty of anything, but is born into a world where death and the pull toward wrong are already in the air. Guilt, in Orthodox teaching, is for sins a person actually commits. Here's what both readings refuse to say: that a person is worthless. Before the garden, Genesis says God looked at everything he had made, "and, behold, it was very good." The fall doesn't undo that. Wounded, in every telling. Worthless, in none.

Think back over the last day, without hunting for your worst moment, and find one small place where you felt a tug you didn't want to follow: impatience, a little lie, wanting to be first. Look at it the way a doctor looks at a bruise, honestly and without disgust, and name it quietly. If you pray, hold it out to God and ask for healing; if not, let it be seen, and breathe with it.
Original sin. The sin at the origin, and what it left in us. Augustine said guilt; the Orthodox say mortality and a wounded nature.
Your line: wounded, not worthless. The wound is real, and so is the very good. See you tomorrow.

1077.title: Augustine and Pelagius
1077.hook: can we be good without grace? Augustine said no; Pelagius was judged to say yes
1077.howItsDone: Western churches, Catholic and Protestant, teach that God's grace comes before any good a person does, following Augustine against Pelagius, and some Christians pray for help before beginning a task or a day's work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, original sin: Augustine said inherited guilt, the Orthodox said mortality and a wound. Your line was wounded, not worthless.

One short line in a prayer started a long quarrel. In his Confessions, Augustine says to God, more or less: give what you command, and then command whatever you will. If you want me to be good, you'll have to give me the goodness first. Augustine himself later wrote that a monk named Pelagius, said to have come from Britain, heard that line and couldn't stand it. To Pelagius it sounded like an excuse, as if people could sit back and wait for God to make them good. Their argument filled books. Today: Augustine and Pelagius.

The question underneath is simple to ask: can a person be good without grace? Grace, here, means God's help, freely given, not earned. Pelagius was a serious man who wanted Christians to live what they said they believed. God gave us free will and the commandments, he argued, and God doesn't command the impossible. So we can obey, and we're responsible when we don't. When he spoke of grace, he pointed to gifts already given: our nature, the law, the example of Jesus. Augustine saw a wound left untreated. In his reading, the human will itself is bent, and a bent will can't straighten itself any more than a broken leg can set itself. So grace has to come first, not as a reward for trying, but as the healing that makes trying possible. He leaned on Jesus's words in John's Gospel: "for without me ye can do nothing." Church councils sided with Augustine, and Pelagius's teaching was condemned. Some historians think Pelagius was more careful than his opponents made him sound, since some of his words reach us through their quotations: worth remembering whenever the winners of an argument describe the losers. And Paul gave both men a verse to hold. Philippians: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do." Churches still balance those two sentences differently. But the West's answer, after that long argument, was grace first.
screen: `WORK IT OUT; GOD WORKS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing waiting for you today that you'd rather avoid, a hard email, a dull chore, a conversation you've put off, and notice how much of you wants to do it well and how much doesn't. If you pray, you can ask God for help with that one task, by name. If you don't, notice that you won't do it entirely on your own: someone taught you, someone fed you, something got you this far.

Your line: grace first. The healing comes before the trying. Until tomorrow.

1078.title: Predestination
1078.hook: Calvin and the Reformed stress God's sovereign choosing; they find comfort in it
1078.howItsDone: Reformed and Presbyterian churches teach predestination in their confessions and catechisms, and some members learn the Heidelberg Catechism's first question and answer, on comfort in life and death, by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine and Pelagius: can we be good without grace? Your line was grace first.

What is your only comfort in life and in death? That's the first question of the Heidelberg Catechism, a teaching book of the Reformed churches, and children in some Reformed congregations learn it by heart. The answer, put simply: that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. Notice the word at the heart of the question. Comfort. Not argument, not fear. Some people hear today's word as cold, even frightening. The people who hold it closest speak of it as comfort. Today: predestination.
screen: `YOUR ONLY COMFORT IN LIFE AND DEATH?`
`A COLD WORD, OR A WARM ONE?`

segments.voice: The word is in the Bible. Paul writes in Romans: "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son." And in Ephesians: "he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world." Yesterday, Augustine said grace must come first. John Calvin and the Reformed churches after him followed that line all the way back. If grace comes first, they said, then before any of us chose God, God chose us. Salvation rests on God's choosing, not on our deciding well. They call this God's sovereignty: God is God, and God's purposes don't fail. Here's where the warmth comes in: Reformed Christians speak of this as comfort. If my hold on God depended on me, they say, it would be as shaky as I am on a bad day. If it depends on God's choosing, it's as steady as God. Jesus says of his sheep, in John's Gospel: "neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Not a ladder you have to keep climbing, but a hand that won't let go. The doctrine raises hard questions, and Reformed teachers admit it: what about those not chosen? Some answer with humility, and leave the question with God. Other Christians answer it differently, and tomorrow we'll hear them. This week, then: a dance, a world from nothing, a fossil, an image, a wound, an argument about grace, and now a hand. Seven ways of asking who God is, and who we are.

Sit back so the chair takes your whole weight, let your shoulders drop, and feel the floor holding you without any help from you. Notice how much effort you usually spend keeping yourself together, and set some of it down. If you pray, rest in the line from John, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand; if you don't, let the chair and the floor hold you, and let that be enough.
Predestination. God choosing before we choose. Calvin and the Reformed churches stress it, and they speak of it as a comfort: held by a hand that won't let go.
Your line: held by his choosing. For those who hold it, a comfort. Same time tomorrow.
